statement: In 12 healthy adults with hallucinogen experience given single high doses of dextromethorphan (DXM) in a supportive laboratory (one double-blind study with a placebo session and DXM doses rising across sessions to each person's stop point), DXM compared with placebo is associated with impaired balance and hand-eye coordination that lasted longer than the impairment after the sedative triazolam and, at the two highest doses each person received, was still present at the last movement test of the session, after the peak effects had begun to fade; at the highest doses some people could not do the tasks at all. Vomiting was common at the higher doses (7 of 12 people; none after placebo or triazolam). No movement test was given after that last test and nobody was tested the next day, so the study does not show when impairment ended; the authors' statement that effects resolved by the end of the session rests on questionnaires, not on movement tests. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
plain: In a laboratory study, twelve experienced volunteers took high doses of DXM on some days, a sleeping pill on other days and a dummy pill on one day. With DXM, balance and hand-eye coordination were affected for longer than with the sleeping pill, and at the highest doses each person took they were still affected at the last test of the day, after the strongest effects had started to fade. Most people vomited at the higher doses. Testing stopped there, so the study cannot say when people were back to normal, and nobody was tested the next day.
population: Healthy adults aged 20 to 40 (9 men, 3 women) with LSD and psilocybin experience, without substance dependence and without personal or family psychotic or bipolar illness, prepared and monitored in a living-room-like laboratory
exposure: Single oral doses of dextromethorphan rising across sessions up to each person's stop point (amounts are study conditions in the study card)
comparator: The same people's placebo session and two triazolam sessions
outcome: Balance and hand-eye coordination (Circular Lights) at repeated tests during the session; vomiting
magnitude: Balance and Circular Lights deficits significantly different from placebo at the last in-session test at each person's penultimate and maximum DXM doses; complete task failure at times at the highest doses; DXM deficits lasted longer than triazolam's. Vomiting in 2 of 12 at the third DXM dose level and in 7 of 12 at the fourth level or above; none after placebo, triazolam or the two lowest DXM doses. Peak psychomotor values are in a supplementary table not read.

evidence.page: Results › Time-course of drug effects; Figure 1
evidence.locator: Results › Time-course of drug effects; Figure 1 legend
evidence.extracted: Effects generally significant by the 2-hour test (the first post-dose psychomotor test), maximal at 2 to 4 hours and decreasing at the 6-hour test, the last; DXM produced longer-lasting Balance and Circular Lights deficits than triazolam; at the penultimate and maximum DXM doses, deficits were still apparent at the last assessment; the highest doses sometimes produced complete impairment (scored 0).

No vomiting after placebo, triazolam or the two lowest DXM doses; 2 of 12 vomited at the third dose level and 7 of 12 at the fourth level or above; vomiting at one dose did not always predict vomiting at the next.

evidence.page: Abstract; Materials and Methods › General Procedures
evidence.locator: Abstract › Results; Materials and Methods › General Procedures, 4th paragraph; Discussion, 7th paragraph
evidence.extracted: The abstract states that drug effects resolved without significant adverse effects by the end of the session; the end-of-session measures, taken when acute effects were judged to have resolved, were questionnaires, and psychomotor tasks were last given at the final in-session test.

evidence.page: Materials and Methods › General Procedures; Data Analysis
evidence.locator: Materials and Methods › General Procedures, 5th paragraph; Data Analysis, 1st paragraph
evidence.extracted: Doses within each drug always rose and escalation stopped when a person could not complete a psychomotor and a computer task, or when the participant or investigator judged a higher dose inadvisable; data were missing at stop-point sessions.

risk_of_bias.note: Ascending, non-randomized dose order; missing data at stop-point sessions; recognisable active conditions.

indirectness.note: Worded for single laboratory doses in screened, experienced volunteers; over-the-counter combination products were not studied.

imprecision.note: Twelve people, two to ten at the highest dose levels; no intervals.

grade.reasoning: A placebo-controlled within-person study with counterbalanced drug-type order starts high, but doses rose in a fixed order. Risk of bias -2 (dose confounded with session order; expectancy and a supportive setting; missing data at stop points). Imprecision -2 (12 people, fewer at the highest doses; values in a supplement not read). Very low. Single study.
